title: Profile lines against reference data: does it match experiment or DNS?
summary: Mean velocity profile in wall units on a log axis, with two model curves and the reference as open markers, and a small inset of the deviation. The standard check of a turbulence model against DNS or experiment.

media.alt: Mean velocity profile in wall units on a log x axis with two model curves and open circles for DNS reference and a small deviation inset.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Does it match experiment or DNS?
read_the_figure.axes: x: y+ = y u_tau / nu, wall distance in wall units, log scale from 1 to 1000. y: u+ = U / u_tau, mean velocity in wall units, linear. Inset: deviation from the reference, linear.
look_at: Is the reference (open circles) on a straight line for y+ above about 30? That is the log law.
Where do model A and model B depart from the markers, and in which direction?
Do the markers follow u+ = y+ for y+ below about 5?
What does the inset say? Does its sign convention match the main panel?
read_the_figure.proves: A model whose profile lies on the markers over the whole range reproduces the mean wall layer: viscous sublayer, buffer layer and log law. It does not prove anything about turbulence quantities like Reynolds stresses, which need their own profiles.
if_wrong: A shifted log line: the additive constant B is wrong, usually a wall-treatment issue.
A different slope in the log region: the von Karman constant effectively differs.
Reference drawn as a line and model as a line: the comparison cannot show the sampling of the data.

terms.meaning: Velocity and distance made dimensionless with the friction velocity and the viscosity: u+ = U/u_tau, y+ = y u_tau/nu.
u_tau = sqrt(tau_w / rho), the velocity scale of the near-wall turbulence.
In the overlap layer u+ = (1/kappa) ln y+ + B, with kappa about 0.41 and B about 5.2.
Region very near the wall where viscous stress dominates and u+ = y+.
Direct numerical simulation: the Navier-Stokes equations solved without a turbulence model; a numerical reference.

remember: Wall units remove the Reynolds number: profiles from different flows collapse.
Sublayer y+ < 5: u+ = y+. Log layer y+ > 30: u+ = 2.44 ln y+ + 5.2.
Reference as open markers, model as lines; both on the same axes.
Always state the sign of the deviation: model minus reference.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position along the log x axis encodes y+, along y encodes u+. Solid teal and dashed blue lines are two models, and open amber circles are the reference. The inset repeats the markers' deviation from the reference line on a zero baseline (rose). Line style and marker shape distinguish the series, not colour alone.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: The wall layer is where models differ and where gradients are largest. A log y+ axis stretches the thin viscous and buffer region and compresses the outer layer, so the log law becomes a straight line and a departure from it is visible. Showing the reference as markers and the model as a line keeps data and model apart and shows how densely the reference is sampled.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Where does the profile switch from u+ = y+ to the log law? The reference sits on the line u+ = y+ at y+ = 1 and 2 (u+ about 1 and 2.5), bends through the buffer layer, and is on a straight line from y+ of about 30; at y+ = 100 it reads about 16.3, and at y+ = 1000 about 22. Q2: Which model is better? Model A passes through all the markers; model B is lower in the buffer layer (below y+ = 10) and about 1 unit above the markers at y+ = 1000 (23 against 22). Q3: What is the log-law slope? From 16.3 at y+ = 100 to 22 at 1000 the rise is 5.7 per decade, that is 5.7/2.303 = 2.5 per e-fold, matching 1/kappa = 2.44.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Reference as markers: the points are the data, with their own sampling; a model is a smooth curve through them or it is not. Drawing both as lines hides the sparse sampling and any scatter.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A log axis makes errors of one or two wall units look small: a 1 unit offset at u+ = 22 is only about 4.5 percent, but it is a visible 4.5 percent in the figure and a large error in the skin friction. The match is also only a mean-velocity match; two models can agree here and differ in turbulence intensity. If the deviation inset has the opposite sign convention to the main panel (it does in this render: model B lies above the markers in the main panel, but its inset curve is negative), the reader is misled. Reference at different Reynolds numbers cannot be compared.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A premultiplied plot y+ du+/dy+ shows the log region as a flat line and magnifies departures. A residual plot over its own axis is cleaner than an inset. Plots of Reynolds stress and TKE profiles complete the comparison.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Replace the inset with a panel sharing the log axis, plot the premultiplied indicator function, and state the sign: model minus reference.

worked.title: Log law at y+ = 100 and 1000
worked.problem: With kappa = 0.41 and B = 5.2, compute u+ at y+ = 100 and y+ = 1000, and the relative offset of a model that reads 23 at y+ = 1000.

solution.text: Log law at the two stations.

worked.answer: 16.4 and 22.0 (the render's markers read about 16.3 and 22.0); model B is high by about 4 percent at y+ = 1000.

analyze.q: The reference follows u+ = y+ for y+ below 5 but model B is lower there. What could the cause be?
Why is the inset deviation useful and why is its sign convention so important?
analyze.hint: If the sign is reversed what would you conclude?

evaluate.q: Is agreement with DNS on u+ enough to select a turbulence model for a heat-transfer problem?
evaluate.hint: What else does heat transfer depend on?

Plot the same profiles in outer scaling (y/delta, U/U_e). What is hidden in which version?

checks.q: Why is the x axis logarithmic?
checks.hint: The near-wall region is very thin.
checks.answer: It stretches the thin viscous and buffer region and turns the log law into a straight line.

checks.q: Compute u+ at y+ = 50 with kappa = 0.41 and B = 5.2.
The inset shows model B negative while the main panel shows it above the markers. What do you conclude?
checks.answer: The inset has a different sign convention (or an error) than the main panel; the figure must state model minus reference and use the same sign in both. Until then you cannot use the inset.
